chapter: Will Marion Cook and the Southern Syncopated Orchestra
title: Bechet joins within 48 hours; how he worked without reading
summary: Cook hired Bechet at once; he could not read, so he played blues solos and filled in with quartets, and Briggs later saw him correct pianist Pierre de Caillaux's harmony.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Sidney Bechet: the man, the horn, the legend

blocks.x: So, he obviously then would have responded to Bechet. And he immediately wanted Bechet in the band; is that right?
Bechet -- did I say, I think I mentioned, in 48 hours, Bechet was
Briggs
with us.
He said, he just said, "Come on, I want you with us?"
Yes, sure.
"I'll pay you so much."
"I'll pay you so much," and Bechet, naturally he was tickled to go.
He was.
Oh, yes.
Well, now, but he couldn't read music, how did he work in the band.

He couldn't read -- you see, we used him as a solo, playing just blues, as a soloist, playing just the blues. And then certain other, when we played numbers like "medleys," or something, we played Dvorak's "Hungarian Rhapsody," he didn't play. He didn't play. He only played in
Briggs
some of the jazz numbers on the program. You see, that's why I'm sorry, I haven't got the program.
Right. So he had a little solo spot?
He did his solo spot and he did a little filling in, with the quartets, which he could feel the harmony in here, in the piano, because he was gifted that way.
Most of us are, if you play jazz you have to be. (Laughter).
Right.

Yes, Bechet was a curious fine person, but there are some things about Sid. He didn't know music, but he would sit at the piano, and play some of the most beautiful things, you know, from what he heard. And not only that, piano player, I've seen him and I've heard him when he played with Benny Peyton's orchestra in the Palais de Hammersmith. We were right opposite. I said, "Not very
Briggs
good colored Dixieland band. The only thing that was good about them was the name. (Laughter). That's why I'm concerned.

You need to listen to Bechet. He would be opposite with the Jazz Kings, Benny Peyton's Jazz Kings, and his piano player, at the time he was a terrific musician, by the name of Pierre de Caillaux, and he was French Canadian, and he, Bechet would, after a number, he would go to Caillaux and say, 'You changed the harmony in this, that spot, and that spot, and that spot.' Caillaux, then after an argument would say, 'Yes, you're right, I did not play the harmony.'
I see.
But Sidney would really have -- he really knew the music in his head?
Oh, yes. A natural musician.
